lesson.title: Change the layout without losing the meaning

steps.headline: pivot turns a long list into a grid, and each cell needs exactly one record.

lead.text: df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units') puts shops down the side and months across the top. Each shop and month pair must appear once, because a cell can hold one value.
A pivot rearranges the observations. It does not change them.
Labels are not cells. A grid holds one measurement for each shop and month combination.

reveal.text: You counted the cells as shops times months. The pivot only rearranges the records into that grid.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 5, 3, 7]})
result = df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
month  Feb  Jan
shop           
Bay      5    2
Hill     7    3

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 5, 3, 7]})
result = df.pivot(index='month', columns='shop', values='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
shop   Bay  Hill
month           
Feb      5     7
Jan      2     3

steps.headline: Two Bay and Jan records have units 5 and 11. What does pivot_table with aggfunc='sum' put in that cell?

lead.text: pivot_table can combine records that share a cell. You choose the combining rule with aggfunc.

workedSteps.text: Both records map to the same Bay and Jan cell, so one value must be made from them.
Apply the chosen rule. With sum the cell is the total.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Jan', 'Jan'], 'units': [2, 6, 3]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='sum')

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Jan', 'Jan'], 'units': [2, 6, 3]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='mean')

steps.headline: Two Bay and Jan records have units 3 and 9. What does aggfunc='sum' produce?

workedSteps.text: How many records land in the Bay and Jan cell?
Apply sum to those records. What is the cell value?

steps.headline: melt turns a grid back into a long list, with one row per measurement.

lead.text: df.melt(id_vars='shop', value_vars=['Jan', 'Feb']) keeps shop beside every value and stacks the month columns into a variable column and a value column. id_vars names the columns that stay attached.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'Jan': [2, 3], 'Feb': [5, 7]})
result = df.melt(id_vars='shop', value_vars=['Jan', 'Feb'], var_name='month', value_name='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
shop month  units
0   Bay   Jan      2
1  Hill   Jan      3
2   Bay   Feb      5
3  Hill   Feb      7

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'Jan': [2, 3], 'Feb': [5, 7]})
result = df.melt(id_vars='shop', value_vars=['Feb'], var_name='month', value_name='units')

values.name: result
values.display:
shop month  units
0   Bay   Feb      5
1  Hill   Feb      7

lead.text: Each original row gives one long row for every value column that is melted.

reveal.text: Every original row contributed one long row per melted column, so the rows multiplied. No measurement was lost, only moved.

lead.text: A pivot has a cell for every shop and month. If no record exists for a pair, that cell is missing. fill_value=0 would call it zero, which is only right when no record truly means none.

reveal.text: The cells without records stayed missing. Filling them with zero would have claimed that nothing was sold, which the data did not say.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 7]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='sum')

values.name: result
values.display:
month  Feb  Jan
shop           
Bay    NaN  2.0
Hill   7.0  NaN

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 7]})
result = df.pivot_table(index='shop', columns='month', values='units', aggfunc='sum', fill_value=0)

values.name: result
values.display:
month  Feb  Jan
shop           
Bay      0    2
Hill     7    0

lesson.orientation: Pivot unique records, aggregate duplicate keys and melt columns back into observations.
lesson.reviewLabel: Change the layout without losing the meaning
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A list has one row for every combination of shop and month. There are 2 shops, and each has a figure for each of 3 months.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a long list into a grid and back, and know what to do when two records land in one cell.

recap.keyIdea: pivot arranges records in a grid when each cell has one record, pivot_table combines repeats with a chosen rule, and melt returns the grid to a list.

blocks.text: You counted 6 rows for 2 shops and 3 months. You found 12 cells in a 3 by 4 grid, and 2 missing cells where no record existed.

recap.nextHook: Next: bring the whole toolkit together in one audited sales report.

questions.prompt: A complete pivot has three shops and four month columns. How many measurement cells does it contain?
hints: Count the grid cells without the labels.
Labels are not measurement cells.
Multiply the shops by the month columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the three shops has four monthly cells, giving 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each of the three shops has a cell for each of the four months.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the shops and months. Each combination has its own cell.

questions.prompt: What cell value does pivot_table with aggfunc='sum' produce?
hints: Apply the rule you were given.
Both records map to the same cell.
Add the two unit values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The duplicate key pair is aggregated as 3 + 9 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Sum combined the two records that share the cell.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. The rule here is sum.
That is only one of the records. The cell combines both.

questions.prompt: Why does pivot fail when one shop and month pair has two records?
hints: One output cell needs a single value.

acceptedIdeas: The requested cell is not uniquely identified
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pivot does not choose an aggregation for ambiguous cells.

choices.label: The requested cell is not uniquely identified
The table must have at least ten rows

questions.onCorrect: The cell is not uniquely identified. pivot does not choose how to combine two records.

misconceptions.feedback: pivot works on tables of any size. The problem is repeated pairs.
Values are usually numbers. Duplicate pairs are the problem.

questions.prompt: Which melt argument names the columns that stay attached to every measurement?
hints: Keep the identifier beside each resulting row.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: id_vars retains identifier columns while selected value columns are unpivoted.

questions.onCorrect: id_vars. It keeps identifier columns attached while the value columns are stacked.

misconceptions.feedback: aggfunc belongs to pivot_table and chooses how to combine.

questions.prompt: A four-row table melts three measurement columns. How many long-form rows result?
hints: Count one row for each melted cell.
Each original row supplies three measurements.
Multiply the rows by the melted columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each original row contributes three measurements, producing 4 × 3 = 12 rows.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each of the four rows gives one long row for each of the three columns.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the counts. Each row gives a long row per column.

questions.prompt: Repeated records have values 4 and 10. What does aggfunc='mean' produce?
hints: The rule is mean, not sum.
Add the two values.
Divide by how many values there are.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The mean of the two repeated records is their total shared equally.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum. The rule here is the mean.

hints: All three records map to one cell.
The rule is sum.
Add the three values.
questions.prompt: Three Bay and Jan records have units 1, 2 and 6. What does pivot_table with aggfunc='sum' put in that cell?
questions.onCorrect: 9. The three records share a cell, and sum combined them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean. The rule here is sum.

hints: There is one row for each shop and month pair.
Every shop has a figure for every month.
Multiply the shops by the months.
questions.prompt: How many rows does the list have?
questions.onCorrect: 6. One row for each shop and month pair. A pivot would lay those same six figures out as a 2 by 3 grid.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the shops and months. There is a row for every pair.

choices.label: Two records share one cell, so a combining rule is needed

acceptedIdeas: Two records share one cell, so a combining rule is needed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pivot_table aggregates records that share a cell.

questions.onCorrect: Two records share one cell, so a combining rule is needed. pivot_table lets you name it.

misconceptions.feedback: pivot handles numbers. It cannot combine repeated cells.
Sorting is not the reason. The shared cell is.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Both records belong to the same cell, which is why a combining rule is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: There are two records for this one cell.

Multiply the shops by the month columns.
questions.prompt: A table has 5 shops, each with a Jan and a Feb column. Melting both month columns gives how many long rows?
questions.onCorrect: 10. Each of the five shops gives one long row per month column.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of shops. Each month gives its own row.
That adds the counts. Each shop gives a row for each month.

questions.prompt: Rows exist only for (Bay, Jan) and (Hill, Feb). A pivot of shops by months has how many cells with no record?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A 2 by 2 grid has four cells, and two are filled.

questions.onCorrect: 2. The grid has four cells, and only two have records, so two stay missing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole grid. Two of the cells have records.
Only the combinations that exist get a value. The others stay missing.
